title: The §6.4 ¶2 upload request, as the constructor for it builds one

source.note: composed: this is `Message::upload_request`'s output, for the `ask` recorded as this case's `expect.message.content`. A test in `crates/conformance/tests/` calls the constructor with that string and asserts it still produces exactly this file's `canonical_json`, so the shape is pinned from both ends: the corpus says what an implementation must produce for these bytes, and the test says the constructor produces those bytes. §6.4 ¶2 fixes the shape — "a message with the MessageType field set to 'control', and the first submessage should include a text format request for the end-point to send large uploads" — and `control` is the `MessageType` and not §6.3's boolean, because ¶2 names that field and no other.

input: {"messagetype":"control","format":"text","subformat":"english","content":"Please provide an end-point for large uploads."}

message.content: Please provide an end-point for large uploads.

expect.text: Please provide an end-point for large uploads.
expect.canonical_json: {"messagetype":"control","format":"text","subformat":"english","content":"Please provide an end-point for large uploads."}

notes: `ecma-430/26` records the same shape as a document a peer sent; this one records it as the shape a *constructor* must build, and the difference is which end the case holds. `input` is the constructor's own compact output rather than the indented spelling `/26` uses, so that the bytes a reader compares against the test are the bytes the test compares. The boolean `control` field is absent and its absence is asserted by `canonical_json`: §6.4 names `MessageType`, §6.3 names the boolean, and a constructor that wrote both would be discharging an obligation nobody gave it — `ecma-430/38` is where §6.3 then adds the boolean on top, because the exchange is a control one.
